opening.headline: For even simple requests, it restructures the system to route them to the largest model based on input format and difficulty, thereby dividing requests according to their form and complexity and assigning them to appropriate services to reduce costs.
body: Services that handle simple requests like customer greeting or delivery inquiry, as well as complex requests like contract analysis, using a single large model are common. The implementation is straightforward, but if most requests are simple, most of the cost is spent on performance beyond necessity, leading to unnecessarily delayed responses.

In this class, we first examine how model selection is differentiated based on the form of input and output in multimodal support. Then, we explore the difficulty-based routing structure composed of classifiers, model assignment, and fallback mechanisms, and examine how costs vary depending on request distribution, illustrating these concepts with practical examples.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the principles of multimodal support and difficulty-based routing.
The input can be categorized and assigned to a model based on its form and difficulty.

screens.title: Sending all requests to the largest model.
screens.lead: Read the following scenario and think about where the costs are being incurred.

visual.alt: A diagram showing how both simple and complex requests are processed by a single large model.

paragraphs: There is a customer service operation that handles all requests—from simple inquiries like delivery tracking, business hours information, and personnel interactions to complex refund decisions—using a single largest model. The design is simple and the quality is stable, making it appear reasonable at first glance.

The issue is the composition of the request. If most requests are simple, they can be adequately handled at a lower tier, avoiding the full cost of larger models. Additionally, larger models are generally slower, causing even simple request responses to become delayed. The Claude documentation introduces the concept of assigning tasks such as classification, extraction, and routing to the fastest, smaller tier.

There's one more point. Requests may not arrive solely in text form; they can include images or voice data, which might exceed the capabilities of a single model. This course addresses a structure that categorizes requests by input type and difficulty level and assigns them appropriately to the right model.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If 80% of requests are simple, how much of the cost associated with large models is being spent on performance that is unnecessary? We'll verify this with numbers during the lecture.

screens.outro: First, let's recall how my service requests are structured.

screens.title: Think about whether all requests use the same model.
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Since you're not entering or submitting an answer, take a moment to reflect first and recall my service.

items.prompt: What is the most common type of request per day?
items.answer: The most common type accounts for the majority of costs. When this type is simple, the cost savings are greatest when sent with a lower grade. The order should be to examine and design starting from the most common type.

items.prompt: What kind of type could be problematic?
items.answer: Types with high error costs are generally safer to keep at a higher tier even if their call frequency is low. OpenAI's accuracy optimization documentation also advises first estimating how costly a single failure can be. Routing not only considers cost but also the value of errors.

items.prompt: Are there other types that have input forms different from images or audio?
items.answer: The available models may differ based on the input format. Requests that require only text, requests that require image understanding, and requests that require speech may need to be routed through different paths from the start. Check this point in the next screen.

screens.outro: Let's first examine how the input format influences model selection.

screens.title: Multimodal support: the input format determines the model selected
screens.lead: Select each tab to verify how the model is divided based on input and output formats by company.

tabs.label: Claude
tabs.body: The Claude document states that the current model supports text and image inputs, text outputs, multilingual capabilities, vision, and tool usage. Therefore, from Haiku 5.5 to Fable 5.1, having image input does not differentiate model tiers. Image-based requests can be graded based on difficulty.

tabs.label: Gemini
tabs.body: The Gemini product line separates models based on input and output types. For image generation and editing, Nano Banana series models are used; for voice conversations, Live series models are employed; for text-to-speech synthesis, TTS models are utilized; and for transcribing speech into text, dedicated Transcribe models exist. These are distinct from the Flash series models, which handle both text and image understanding. In other words, if a request involves both image generation and speech, it cannot be addressed by a single model.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: OpenAI documentation indicates that model availability, tools, reasoning settings, and usage limits may vary depending on the product and model version. Even models with the same name may offer different tools and settings, so it is safe to first identify the required features and then select the appropriate model that supports those features.

tabs.label: Routing criteria
tabs.body: The commonality among the three companies is that the form of input and output serves as a condition for model selection. Whether a request involves images, speech, or generation becomes the first criterion, followed by difficulty level. Therefore, routing rules typically begin by branching based on form, and then divide requests within the same form into simple and complex ones.

screens.outro: We will examine the structure broken down by form and then categorized by difficulty, component by component.

screens.title: Routing structure by difficulty level: Classifier, model assignment, fallback
screens.lead: Select the number marker on the diagram to view detailed information about each component. Please check them in order from number 1, following the sequence in which requests flow.

visual.alt: The request is routed through a classifier to either a small model or a large model, with a failover routing structure where failures of the small model are redirected to the large model.

markers.label: Classifier
markers.title: Classifier: Divides requests into easy and difficult categories.
markers.body: The classifier is a rule or a small model that determines which model to send based on assessing the difficulty or type of the request. It can start with keyword rules or request length, or it can delegate classification to a small model. Classifiers also incur costs and errors, so it is necessary to separately verify whether the classification result is correct.

markers.label: Low grade
markers.title: Small-grade model: Basic path for simple requests
markers.body: Simple requests are sent quickly and affordably using small tiers. The OpenAI guide recommends starting with smaller models and upgrading only when accuracy is insufficient, thereby reducing both cost and delay. The Claude documentation also introduces Haiku 5.5 as a starting point for tasks such as classification, extraction, and routing.

markers.label: High grade
markers.title: High-grade model: Path for difficult requests
markers.body: Composite judgments or requests with high error costs are assigned a high priority. Although the number of calls is small, the value of each request is high, justifying the cost. A high priority also serves as the last line of defense to maintain the overall quality of routing.

markers.label: Fallback
markers.title: fallback: if failed, resend with a larger model
markers.body: Fallback is an alternative path that sends requests back to a higher-level model when a smaller model's output fails to meet the standard or when the call fails. Having this mechanism helps reduce the risk of poor quality in requests sent to the smaller model. However, if fallback occurs frequently, the same request may be processed twice, reducing the overall efficiency.

markers.label: Form verification
markers.title: Input format verification: criterion taught before difficulty level
markers.body: Whether the request involves images, audio, or generation must be confirmed prior to difficulty assessment. This is because grade assignments can only be made within a predefined model based on its form. This confirmation can be easily handled by establishing rules before the classifier.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the structure, let's look at numerical examples to see how costs change when request distribution varies.

screens.title: Cost changes by request distribution
screens.lead: Try adjusting the ratio of simple requests using the slider. The relative cost compared to processing each request with a single large model is displayed. The assumed unit price ratio is listed in the screen description.

visual.alt: Bar chart showing that as the proportion of simple requests increases, the relative cost of routing becomes significantly lower compared to a single-model configuration.
labels: Assumption: small model cost 0.1, classification cost 0.02, fallback 10%

stops.body: Assumption: Set the cost per request for a large model to 1, for a small model to 0.1, and for a classifier to 0.02 per request. Additionally, 10% of requests routed to the small model are fallbacks that re-route to the large model. If simple requests account for only 20%, the relative cost becomes 0.02 + 0.2×0.1 + 0.2×0.01×1 + 0.8 = 0.86. The cost reduction is only 14%, and the classifier cost and fallback significantly reduce the savings. Under this distribution, the benefit of introducing routing is minimal.

Under the same assumption, the relative cost is 0.02 + 0.5×0.1 + 0.5×0.1 + 0.5 = 0.62. This is 38% lower than a large model single configuration. While half the simplicity leads to noticeable cost savings, half of difficult requests still account for most of the cost.

The relative cost is 0.02 + 0.7×0.1 + 0.7×0.01 + 0.3 = 0.46. It drops to half of the large model's single configuration. As the number of simple requests increases, the proportion of fixed costs such as classification and fallback decreases, and the cost reduction becomes more significant.

The relative cost is 0.02 + 0.9×0.1 + 0.9×0.01 + 0.1 = 0.30. This represents only about 30% of the cost of a large model's single configuration. Since the accuracy of the classifier and the fallback rate determine the overall cost savings, these two metrics must be continuously measured. From a Google Cloud cost optimization perspective, it is recommended to start with a small scale and scale resources up to an appropriate size based on actual requirements.

screens.outro: Let's explore a service where 80% of requests are simple by using this calculation.

screens.title: 80% of service routing explanations are simply requests.
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down the routing design for customer consultation services step by step. Select an arrow to advance one step at a time, following the design sequence.

steps.title: Situation: 80% of inquiries are simple queries in the consultation service.
steps.body: We offer customer service support. Eighty percent of inquiries are simple queries such as shipment tracking or business hours, while twenty percent involve complex requests like refund justification or interpretation of terms and conditions. Currently, all requests are being sent to a large model, but there has been a request to reduce monthly costs due to the expense. All figures are assumed for illustrative purposes only.

steps.title: Step 1. Distribution measurement
steps.body: Before designing routing, first verify the proportions and difficulty levels from logs. The figure of 80% must be measured, not estimated. Without measurement, you won't know whether the actual distribution is 50% or 90%, and as seen on the previous screen, the reduction rate can vary significantly. At this time, also display error types that carry high error costs.

steps.title: Step 2. Model Assignment
steps.body: 80% simple requests are routed to lower-tier models, while 20% complex requests are sent to higher-tier models. The classifier begins with simple rules such as request length or keywords; when accuracy is insufficient, it delegates classification to a smaller model. Requests with different formats—such as those containing images—are first branched off at the classifier stage and routed to the appropriate model.

steps.title: Step 3. Cost Calculation
steps.body: When the large model is used at 100%, setting the cost per request to 1 results in a relative routing cost of 0.02 + 0.8×0.1 + 0.8×0.01 + 0.2 = 0.38 on the assumption screen. This is approximately 62% lower than when using only the large model. This value depends on the assumed unit pricing ratio and fallback ratio, so it must be recalculated using actual pricing and measured fallback rates.

steps.title: Step 4. fallback and Quality Verification
steps.body: If a small model fails or falls short of the standard, the request is escalated to a larger model. The classifier evaluates the ratio of misclassifications by checking whether easy requests are incorrectly classified as hard ones, or vice versa. Misclassifications where hard requests leak into the small model lead to quality degradation, while misclassifications where easy requests are incorrectly routed to the large model result in wasted costs.

screens.outro: Finally, let's summarize the core of this lesson.

screens.title: Request distribution is the basis of routing.
screens.lead: Let's summarize the key points of this class. Please revisit the questions posed on the problem presentation screen.

paragraphs: The starting point of routing is the distribution of requests. We must measure how many of each type there are, how difficult each type is, and the cost when they are incorrect. Without such measurements, we cannot determine the potential savings or risks of routing.

Model allocation is based on two criteria. First, we assess whether the input and output types include image, speech, or generation. Second, within the same type, we categorize by difficulty level. Currently, all Claude models support image input, making difficulty the primary criterion. However, separate models are required for image generation or speech within different product lines. The classifier divides requests, while fallback mechanisms ensure quality.

Going back to the initial question, assuming that 80% of requests are simple, designing a single large model to handle all of them results in spending a significant portion of cost on unnecessary performance. Under the same assumption, routing reduces relative cost to a level of 0.38. However, as the proportion of simple requests decreases, the cost savings from classification and fallback mechanisms diminish. The accuracy of the classifier and the fallback rate must be continuously measured after implementation.

The recommended order when starting design is fixed. Measure types and difficulty from request logs, divide paths by form and difficulty, calculate relative costs based on assumed unit prices, and then verify routing gains using evaluation sets for fallback rates and classification accuracy. Following this order allows routing benefits to be quantified numerically.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: The price ratios, classification costs, and fallback rates in this lesson are illustrative assumptions. In a real design, calculate them using current prices and measured values.

checks.intro: Recall the cost change you just saw and verify it for yourself. The results are not recorded.
checks.q: Introducing difficulty-based routing for services with low simple request ratios resulted in cost savings that were less than expected. What is the most appropriate reason?
options: The smaller model always has more calls than the larger model.
Routing costs only decrease when the input forms are identical.
The classifier avoids backtracking because it accurately filters all simple requests.
Classification incurs costs, and since small models fail on certain requests, those requests must be forwarded to larger models, reducing overall benefit.
checks.explain: The greater the number of simple requests, the larger the savings; with fewer requests, classification costs and fallback reinvocations reduce the savings.

wrong.0: Call frequency and grade pricing are different issues.
wrong.1: The input format indicates only the assignment reference date and does not indicate whether reduction has occurred.
wrong.2: Classification faults may occur, and fallback is actually a safety mechanism that preserves quality.

checks.intro: Now recall the design sequence just explained and arrange it appropriately. The result is not recorded.
checks.q: For a service where 80% of requests are simple inquiries like delivery tracking, please review the routing design process in the correct sequence.
items: Measures type ratios and difficulty from logs
Simple requests are assigned a low level, while composite requests are assigned a high level.
Calculates cost against a full 100% large model
Only failed small-model samples are promoted to the large model and their quality is verified using the evaluation set.
checks.explain: First, we must understand the distribution to perform allocation; then, with allocation in place, we can calculate the cost; finally, we verify the fallback and quality.

glossary.def: The ability to handle various forms such as images and audio, not just text, as input or output.
This is a structure that assigns models of different grades based on the difficulty of the request.
A rule or small model that determines which model to send based on assessing the difficulty or type of the request.
This is an alternative path that sends the result of a smaller model back to a larger model when the smaller model's output fails to meet the criteria or succeeds.

misconceptions.fact: When the proportion of simple requests is low, the benefit is reduced due to classification costs and fallback reinvocation. Under the assumptions of this course, the reduction was only 14% when simple requests accounted for 20%.
Classification errors directly lead to quality degradation or wasted costs. Since classification incurs both cost and errors, its accuracy must be measured separately.

misconceptions.myth: All models receive the same input.
misconceptions.fact: Models support different formats such as images, audio, and generation. Gemini provides image generation and speech separately through dedicated models.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Request distribution serves as the basis for routing, and it must be measured to determine the savings.
First, observe the input and output formats, and then assign difficulty levels to the model.
The classifier divides requests and fallback ensures quality.
The higher the ratio of simple requests, the greater the savings; conversely, when it is low, the costs of classification and fallback become advantageous.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What proportion of my requests can be adequately served by a small model, and what is the rationale behind this?
